analysis.one_liner: Stops the Pentagon from reimbursing defense contractors for environmental cleanup costs at their own facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and its subcommittee but never received a hearing markup or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law defense contractors can bill the federal government for environmental cleanup costs at facilities they own or operate, or where they are liable for the cleanup under federal environmental law. This bill amends a Pentagon contracting statute to add those costs to the list of expenses the government will not reimburse, and it applies to contracts already in existence as well as future contracts. In effect, contractors with pollution liability would have to pay their own cleanup bills instead of passing them to taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would no longer cover environmental cleanup costs that defense contractors owe under federal pollution law; and communities near contaminated contractor facilities, who would benefit from contractors bearing the true cost of cleanup. The bill text adds these costs to the list of unallowable contract costs and applies to existing and future contracts [S3] [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and residents near contaminated sites

how_it_helps.text: Adds environmental response costs at contractor-owned or contractor-liable facilities to the list of costs the Pentagon cannot reimburse under section 2324(e)(1) of title 10 [S3].
Applies to contracts already in existence on the date of enactment, not just new contracts, so it would not be avoided by rewriting future deals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors, who would absorb environmental cleanup costs they currently pass to the government through contract reimbursements [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: A good-faith objection: contractors sometimes perform environmentally required work at government-owned sites under direction from the government, and a flat prohibition could leave a contractor unable to recover costs it incurred at the government's instruction, since the amendment bars reimbursement at any facility where the contractor is liable in whole or in part [S3].

Contractors could argue the change raises costs or risk on defense work, which defense contractors might pass back through pricing on future contracts; the bill left this unaddressed because it never advanced past committee [S5] [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: shifting cleanup liability back to the polluting contractor versus possible friction in how defense contracts price environmental work. The bill is a narrow, targeted change to one list of unallowable costs, and its main weakness is that a blanket bar could also sweep in costs a contractor incurred at the government's direction; that tension was never examined because the bill stalled in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee, sent to its subcommittee on military installations, and the Pentagon was asked for its views, but nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced November 9, 1993 by Rep. Carolyn Maloney with 4 cosponsors (3 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S1] [S4].
Referred to the House Armed Services Committee on the day of introduction [S5] [S1].

Eleven days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Military Installations and Facilities, and executive comment was requested from the Department of Defense; no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, without a subcommittee or full committee vote and without reaching the House floor [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors, who continued to be reimbursed by the government for environmental cleanup costs at facilities they own or where they are liable, keeping those costs on taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors and their contract reimbursements

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.role: Sponsor, House Armed Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar Pentagon reimbursement of contractors' environmental cleanup costs.

for.name: 3 House Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it initial support in the House.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Ron Dellums (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Military Installations and Facilities and never reported it out, so it never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so there is no recorded party breakdown; the sponsor and all listed cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the committee majority that never advanced it was also Democratic [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to bill the government for environmental cleanup costs at their own or partially liable facilities, shifting those costs back to the companies. Today those cleanup bills are paid by taxpayers under the reimbursement rules the bill targeted [S2] [S3].
